channel.title: Oleksandr Shepotylo
channel.description: What leaving the EU actually did to British trade — measured, not argued.

item.title: After SPS: the EU trade barrier that needs fixing next
item.description:
Drawing on five years of monthly bilateral trade data across 100 countries (2017–2025), this piece finds that while deeply integrated sectors like pharmaceuticals and automotive components have proven more resilient to Brexit than consumer goods, the underlying commercial logic of running cross-border production under two regulatory regimes is weakening year on year. Overall, UK exports to the EU have seen a 53.8% decline in product varieties and a 16.5% fall in value, with technical barriers — conformity assessment and dual certification in particular — imposing disproportionate costs on the most interconnected sectors. The recommendation is a sectoral mutual recognition agreement modelled on the EU–Switzerland framework, alongside investment support for firms absorbing dual regulatory costs, before the window to preserve these cross-border production relationships closes.

Written by Jun Du, based on our joint research on UK–EU trade.

Originally published on British Chambers of Commerce, September 14, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: What steel tariffs reveal about the cost of going it alone
item.description:
Using trade data and economic modelling, this piece with Professor Jun Du examines the UK steel tariffs announced in March 2026. It finds the US tariffs already caused steel imports to fall 20% while consumer prices rose around 27%, with 70–80% of the cost passed on to downstream buyers. The UK’s roughly 300,000 downstream steel-using workers carry a heavier burden than its 30,000 primary steelmakers, and the piece argues the UK should coordinate its trade-defence policy with the EU rather than act alone — a joint approach could generate preferential gains worth roughly £482 million a year.

Originally published on UK in a Changing Europe, April 28, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Beyond Tinkering: Is a “Swiss-Style” Reset Next for UK–EU Trade?
item.description:
Sector-by-sector patches to the Trade and Cooperation Agreement have not reversed the underlying decline in EU–UK trade: exports, and more recently imports, keep falling in both value and the variety of products traded. Regulation-heavy sectors such as chemicals, pharmaceuticals and medical devices are hit hardest, carrying duplicate compliance costs and parallel certification that fragments supply chains. Rather than more sector-specific fixes, the piece argues ministers should treat the relationship as a strategic choice about regulatory alignment — deciding which areas justify following EU rules in exchange for smoother market access — with real consequences for the UK’s long-term growth model.

Originally published on Substack, March 21, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: The UK Trade Report for September 2025
item.description:
A Douglas Adams-inspired look at Britain’s September 2025 trade figures identifies four key trends: a precious-metals trading boom driven by uncertainty over American policy, strong aerospace and defence exports helped by US tariff exemptions, declining automotive exports reflecting deeper structural problems, and Britain’s near-total absence from the AI hardware trade currently driving growth elsewhere. The overall picture is of an economy that excels at financial services and a few niche sectors while steadily losing ground in manufacturing and emerging technology.

Originally published on Substack, November 21, 2025.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Tariff Turbulence: How Trump’s Threats Are Rocking the UK Trade Deal
item.description:
Renewed US tariff threats are undermining the UK-US trade relationship post-Brexit, with UK automotive exports down an estimated 18% and pharmaceuticals down 23%, and risk spreading to entertainment-sector collaboration. The piece reads this instability as exposing how fragile a US-dependent trade strategy is, and argues it strengthens the case for the UK to diversify its trade partnerships rather than treat the US deal as a settled anchor.

Originally published on Substack, October 3, 2025.

Read the full piece →

item.title: UK-US deal? Not so fast!
item.description:
Trump’s tariffs have driven the largest monthly fall in US exports on record (data back to January 1997), and the UK’s Economic Prosperity Deal with Washington hasn’t spared exporters from 25% car tariffs and a 10% general surcharge. Meanwhile, Trade and Cooperation Agreement frictions continue to weigh on UK-EU trade, so the UK is absorbing costs on both its largest trading relationships at once. The piece argues the more reliable fix is closer to home: renegotiating the TCA and deepening EU ties, rather than banking on an unpredictable US partner.

Originally published on Substack, June 12, 2025.

Read the full piece →

item.title: How did the Brexit uncertainty impact services exports of UK firms?
item.description:
Brexit-related uncertainty had a measurable, negative effect on UK firms’ services exports — distinct from, and in some respects larger than, the effect of the tariff and non-tariff barriers that eventually took effect. Using firm-level export data and a synthetic difference-in-differences design, we isolate the uncertainty channel from the trade-policy channel by comparing UK firms to a synthetic control built from firms in countries that faced no comparable shock.

Published in: Journal of International Business Policy, 8(1), 80–104

Aston Research Explorer

item.title: Shocked by COVID: Exporting along global value chains
item.description:
COVID-19 hit firms embedded in global value chains differently depending on their position in the chain — upstream suppliers and downstream assemblers absorbed the shock through different channels. Using UK firm-level export data spanning the pandemic, we trace how GVC position shaped the size and persistence of the export shock, and how much of the disruption has since reversed.

Working paper: CEP Discussion Papers dp2105

Aston Research Explorer

item.title: Trade Disintegration and Agri-Food Trade: United Kingdom Exit From EU
item.description:
We provide a comprehensive difference-in-differences analysis of how the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement affected the UK’s agri-food trade after Brexit. Both the value and quantity of UK agri-food exports and imports fell significantly post-TCA, while prices rose as worsened market access and additional border checks pushed up trade costs. The results underline the importance of legal enforceability in trade agreements — particularly for agricultural and sanitary/phytosanitary provisions — for preserving market access and trade volumes.

Published in: The World Economy, 2025. With Jun Du and Yundan Shi.

Aston Research Explorer / ORCID

item.title: Productivity, trade openness and UK trade policy adventurism
item.description:
The piece argues that the UK’s growth problem is best understood as a competitiveness crisis — high market power combined with low rates of firm entry that together choke off dynamism. ONS data shows markups at record levels (1.27 in 2022) and weak business churn, with what productivity growth there is concentrated among a small set of top-performing firms. The proposed fix is more trade openness: greater competition from abroad would compress prices and spur innovation, and of the available options a customs union with the EU is presented as the most realistic route to restoring market dynamism in the UK’s current protectionist drift.

Originally published on Substack, December 3, 2024.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Brexit and the Services Trade—A Longitudinal Analysis
item.description:
Using the OECD-WTO Balanced Trade in Services dataset and a synthetic difference-in-differences design, we estimate the impact of Brexit uncertainty on UK services trade from 2016 to 2019. UK services exports fell short of a synthetic no-Brexit counterfactual by an average of US$23.7bn (£18.5bn) a year — a 5.65% reduction — with substantial variation across sectors and destinations. Bilateral exports fell by 8.5% on average; large markets such as Germany and the US were less affected than smaller ones, UK exports to the EU as a whole declined by 6.21%, while, strikingly, exports to Ireland expanded by 21.4%.

Published in: Journal of Service Research, 2024. With Jun Du.

Aston Research Explorer / ORCID

item.title: Would a veterinary agreement be a boost for UK-EU agri-food exports?
item.description:
Evidence from 279 trade agreements worldwide shows that comprehensive, legally binding commitments on agricultural standards can substantially expand agri-food trade — in the UK-EU case, potentially raising UK agri-food exports to the EU by 22.5% over ten years. Crucially, the analysis shows this doesn’t require the UK to simply adopt EU rules wholesale: mutual recognition of equivalent standards can deliver the gains. The politics of getting there remain hard, but the piece argues a supplementary veterinary agreement sitting alongside the existing TCA is economically well worth pursuing.

Originally published on UK in a Changing Europe, June 17, 2024.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Economic disintegration: Brexit, Non-tariff Measures, and UK Trade
item.description:
Although the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement established tariff- and quota-free trade in goods, UK-EU trade costs rose significantly after Brexit. Using a synthetic control difference-in-differences design, we show the TCA had a significant, adverse effect on bilateral UK-EU trade, and we quantify the ad valorem equivalents of the non-tariff measures introduced after the Brexit transition period, tracing their impact on UK trade through 2021.

Working paper: Research Square preprint, 2024. With Jun Du.

Aston Research Explorer / ORCID

item.title: Why UK and old Europe have stagnation in productivity growth?
item.description:
Stagnant productivity growth across the UK and Western Europe reflects both long-run and cyclical forces: a slowdown in the arrival of major new technologies, a workforce ageing out of easy retraining, and chronic underinvestment in R&D. On top of that sit two medium-term shocks — Brexit’s reduction of UK trade openness, and the Ukraine war’s disruption of German energy supply — which the piece identifies as the reason the UK’s productivity slump has been unusually severe, tied specifically to its reduced access to global value chains.

Originally published on Substack, August 29, 2023.

Read the full piece →

item.title: GDP Blues: Unravelling the UK’s Troubled Economic Slowdown
item.description:
The UK’s real GDP grew just 0.9% between 2019 and 2023, well behind comparable economies, and this post traces that underperformance to four compounding causes: weak consumer confidence dragging down domestic spending, export growth stalled by new post-Brexit trade barriers, falling imports signalling reduced participation in global supply chains, and a recovery propped up disproportionately by government spending rather than private investment. Fixing the structural issues, not just riding out the cycle, is what the piece argues Britain actually needs.

Originally published on Substack, July 30, 2023.

Read the full piece →

item.title: The impact of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement on UK trade
item.description:
With Jun Du, this piece sets out econometric evidence that the Trade and Cooperation Agreement, in force since January 2021, is a major driver of the UK’s weak trade performance — not a neutral continuity arrangement. Exports to the EU came in 22.1% lower and imports 9.5% lower than a no-Brexit counterfactual would predict, and the UK lost an estimated 20–42% of its export product variety over the first fifteen months, with small firms in manufacturing regions hit hardest.

Originally published on UK in a Changing Europe, June 14, 2023.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Harvesting Trade Opportunities: Staggered DID of Impact and Structural Gravity of Future of EU-UK Agrifood Trade
item.description:
Combining a staggered difference-in-differences estimate of Brexit’s realised impact on EU-UK agrifood trade with a structural gravity projection of plausible future trading arrangements, this paper asks how much of the post-Brexit agrifood trade loss is recoverable under alternative UK-EU relationships, and how much is likely permanent.

Conference paper: International Agricultural Trade Research Consortium

Aston Research Explorer

item.title: How did Brexit affect UK trade?
item.description:
A plain-language stocktake of the UK trade evidence two years after the Trade and Cooperation Agreement took effect, aimed at a policy and social-science audience rather than a specialist trade-economics one. We summarise what the firm- and product-level data show about goods versus services, large firms versus small ones, and which sectors adjusted fastest.

Published in: Contemporary Social Science, 18(2), 266–283

Aston Research Explorer

item.title: UK trade in the time of COVID-19: A review
item.description:
We review the UK’s trade performance through the COVID-19 crisis and consider how it might be revived. UK goods exports contracted more sharply in 2020 than those of international peers, with a deeper decline and slower recovery than Germany, Italy, Spain, and the US. Trends from 2017 to 2019 already showed the UK’s global competitiveness weakening, suggesting a more persistent problem against a backdrop of productivity slowdown and Brexit uncertainty. We analyse the confluence of internal and external factors bearing on UK trade and argue that boosting productivity is central to recovering from both the COVID shock and Brexit.

Published in: The World Economy, 2022. With Jun Du.

Aston Research Explorer / ORCID

item.title: An examination of EU trade disintegration scenarios
item.description:
Using a structural gravity approach, we examine the welfare implications of scenarios in which the EU itself partially disintegrates, rather than just the UK leaving it. The remaining EU countries stand to lose considerably more from EU disintegration than they did from a disorderly Brexit. Some neighbouring high- and middle-income countries — Bosnia and Herzegovina and Norway among them — would actually benefit under certain disintegration scenarios, gaining trade competitiveness relative to the weakened EU bloc.

Published in: The World Economy, 2021. With Karen Jackson.

Aston Research Explorer / ORCID
